title: Dual-precipitates enhance fatigue resistance in an additively manufactured high-entropy alloy
abstract: Abstract To accomplish the intense desire of high-strength materials for enhanced energy-efficiency, recent research applies a combined strategy of additive-manufacturing and precipitation-strengthening in high entropy alloys. In a context, Al 0.2 Co 1.5 CrFeNi 1.5 Ti 0.3  nanoprecipitation-strengthened system was developed, demonstrating very convincing strength and toughness. Moreover, additive-manufacturing facilitated additional strength by well-decorated cell-boundaries with blocky L2 1  precipitates and homogeneously distributed L1 2  precipitates. However, fatigue research of this alloy remained unexplored despite being the main precursor for structural applications. In this study low-cycle fatigue behavior of this alloy in both as-built and precipitation-strengthened (aged) conditions has been explored, combined with in-situ neutron diffraction investigation. Findings revealed a substantial cyclic-stress profile and a notable fatigue-life below ±0.50% strain-amplitude, exceeding 10 5  cycles at ±0.30% strain-amplitude. These demonstrate the potential to carry higher payloads with marked engineering-reliability. Residual-stress estimation revealed strain-compatibility between the matrix and L1 2  precipitate, indicating a crack-initiation immune interface. A comparative examination of dislocation character revealed shifting towards pure edge-character in aged alloy indicates precipitates promoted planar-slip during deformation.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The development and discovery of materials with high mechanical performance have always been in demand for energy efficiency. Great fatigue-resistant materials are the utmost requirement for economics, engineering reliability, and safety for structural applications. Comprising a higher fatigue stress profile and enhanced fatigue life is worthwhile to accomplish higher payload and durability under fluctuating loads. Enhancing fatigue strength is also critical for achieving higher payload and avoiding failures caused by undesirable load fluctuations. The proposed idea of the multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) design and high-entropy effect on phase stability 1 , 2  has revolutionized the exploration of the central region of multi-component phase diagrams, offering great opportunities for the discovery of new and exciting materials. Miracle et al. 3  critically reviewed previous studies and revisited the definition, thermodynamic aspects, and phase-formation trends in high-entropy alloys (HEAs). They proposed a taxonomy for the HEAs, highlighted the vastness and opportunities, outlined the efforts made towards their mechanical and functional applications, and provided broad prospects and future possibilities. The research excitement of these alloys is deeply rooted in their outstanding mechanical attributes, having UTS 1.0 to 1.5 GPa and phase stability in the cryogenic to high-temperature range 3 ,  4 ,  5 – 6 . An early approach of preparing single-phase equiatomic HEAs was restricted by the phase-formation complexity and limited to a certain composition and property range 7 . The idea of leveraging phase complexities to enhance mechanical attributes has shifted the design paradigm towards multi-phase HEAs by varying compositions from equiatomic to non-equiatomic with small substitutions of specific elements and interstitial additions 8 ,  9 – 10 . These strategies resulted in approximately a 20–40% increase in UTS. Besides, for a thorough investigation and prediction, machine-learning and high-throughput approaches have been applied 11 . Currently, acquiring strengthening through precipitates in HEAs has been a recent trend, and a dramatic strengthening effect (approx. 50% increment in UTS) has been reported 12 , 13 . Liu et al. 14  published a dedicated review article on nanoprecipitation-strengthened HEAs and highlighted the impact of several factors on strengthening, such as the type, size, morphology, and distribution of precipitates, and precipitate-matrix interfacial characteristics. The article summarized the effect of various types of precipitate phases observed in HEAs, such as carbides, L1 2 -structured γ ‘  phase, D0 22  structure γ “  phase, B2 phase, σ, and μ intermetallics, on mechanical properties. Among the different types of precipitates, a nanoscale L1 2 -structured γ ‘  phase, which is mostly incorporated in advanced superalloys 15 , furnished an excellent strengthening effect and has therefore been extensively investigated in HEAs 16 . The reported size of the γ ‘  phases in several HEAs are relatively small, ranging from a few to tens of nanometers. Hence, the reduced lattice mismatch is primarily attributed to order-strengthening rather than coherency and modulus strengthening 17 . Yang et al. 18  emphasized the ductile nature of multi-component L1 2  precipitates, which enhanced the dislocation storing capacity and impeded dislocation motion. Admiring those attributes, Zheng et al. 19  introduced an L1 2  phase into the CoCrFeNi system by adding a stoichiometric ratio of Ni 3 Al and observed improvement in the yield strength from 256 MPa to 910 MPa and ultimate tensile strength from 580 MPa to 1200 MPa; however, ductility reduction from 60% to 14%. The highly reactive Al in a Ni 3 Al intermetallic phase is also susceptible to moisture-induced embrittlement 20 . Hence, a vital concern while designing precipitates is to avoid the loss of ductility and environmental embrittlement. A partial substitution of Al by Ti in Ni 3 Al formed a complex Ni 3 (Al, Ti) type of the γ ‘  phase and provided similar strengthening 21 . An increased Ti/Al ratio also improves work hardening due to the increased antiphase-boundary energy, which enhances dislocation cross-slip and microband formation, and hence, extends the uniform deformation 22 ,  23 – 24 . Thus, the Ni 3 (Al, Ti) complex γ ‘  phase in the HEAs has been extensively investigated. Chang et al. 25  studied the phase-property evolutions at different temperatures by the readjustment of  x  and  y  in the Al x Co 1.5 CrFeNi 1.5 Ti y , where  x  +  y  is fixed to 0.5. Among the different Al and Ti combinations, only the Al 0.2  + Ti 0.3  alloy possesses an equilibrium γ ‘  phase with the γ matrix phase. He et al. 12  also demonstrated that a small addition of Al and Ti can produce fine dispersion of L1 2 -type complex Ni 3 (Ti, Al) γ ‘  nano-precipitates and a minor amount of Ni 2 AlTi particles in the CoCrFeNi system by a proper thermo-mechanical treatment. These precipitates contributed to effective strengthening, resulting in an increase of ultimate tensile yield strength from approximately 500 MPa to 1000 MPa while retaining a considerable ductility of 17%. Yang et al. 18  featured the innovative design idea of toughening the multi-component L1 2  by Al–Ti adjustment, controlled by the order-disorder transformation and elemental partitioning, and reported an exceptional strength-ductility combination of ~1.5 GPa UTS and ~50% elongation. Upon applying additive manufacturing (AM), further improvement of ~200 to ~300 MPa in tensile strength of the extensively investigated L1 2 -precipitation-strengthened Al 0.2 Co 1.5 CrFeNi 1.5 Ti 0.3  HEA 26  was noted. The increased strength attributed to AM microfeatures evolved due to rapid and repeated heating-cooling 27 . Recently, the strengthening and fracture resistance role of honeycomb and dislocation-precipitate skeleton structure formed by laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) was reported for Al 0.5 CoCrFeNi HEA 28 , 29 . Lin et al. 26  reported similar features for L-PBF-fabricated Al 0.2 Co 1.5 CrFeNi 1.5 Ti 0.3  HEA upon aging at 750 °C for 50 h. All those reported studies investigated the effects of L1 2  precipitates during monotonic loading. However, most of the catastrophic mechanical failures in real-world scenarios are caused by fatigue. Thus, fatigue-property investigation and understanding of the role of those precipitates under cyclic-deformation is very critical. The fatigue studies of HEAs to date are in a relatively early stage, and very limited literatures are available 30 , especially revealing the role of precipitates on fatigue behavior. Recently, Feng et al. 31  investigated the role of a B2-type precipitate in the LCF behavior of an Al 0.5 CoCrFeNi HEA, and they observed metastability and transformation into a martensitic phase.

Motivated by the enhanced tensile property (~1235 MPa YS and ~1550 MPa UTS) 26  of an L-PBF-fabricated dual nano-precipitate Al 0.2 Co 1.5 CrFeNi 1.5 Ti 0.3  system and the initial stage of HEA-fatigue research, we investigated the LCF behavior. The detailed insights into fatigue deformation and the severity of fatigue crack-initiation due to the additional phase boundary of conventional alloy-design wisdom were investigated. To further elucidate the deformation behavior and the role of nano-precipitates, we also conducted advanced in-situ neutron-diffraction measurements. The micro-level deformation response during LCF loading is explored through line-profile analysis (LPA) of diffraction patterns recorded during in-situ measurement by single-peak fitting (SPF), Rietveld refinement, and convolutional multiple whole profile (CMWP) procedure. To elucidate the impact of precipitates on fatigue properties, we presented a comparative study of as-built (without precipitate) and aged (with precipitate) alloys. The evolved fatigue-stress profile in the aged alloy is much higher (~250 to 400 MPa, depending upon strain amplitude) as compared to the as-built alloy. The stress profile is also higher than various prominent aerospace materials like Ni-based superalloys 32 ,  33 ,  34 ,  35 – 36 , Ti alloys 37 , 38 , stainless steels 39 , 40 , which typically exhibit stress below 1000 MPa at selected strain amplitudes. Additionally, it exhibits a notable fatigue life of ~10 5  cycles or more at strain amplitudes below 0.50%.

sections.heading: Initial microstructural characterization
paragraphs: Images in Fig.  1a, b  show the SEM micrographs of the Al 0.2 Co 1.5 CrFeNi 1.5 Ti 0.3  alloys in both the L-PBF as-built and aged (@750 °C/50 h) conditions. In the as-built state, the micrograph has cellular structures, which is a very inherent feature of L-PBF-printed materials, typically observed in both conventional alloys and HEAs 26 , 41 , 42 . A cell-wall region has a high dislocation density along with segregated Al and Ti atoms 26 . The aged alloy has homogeneously distributed smaller precipitates throughout the matrix and well-decorated blocky particles at the cell-boundary region. The Rietveld refined neutron-diffraction patterns of both alloys presented in Fig.  1c  present only face-centered-cubic (fcc) phase peaks in the as-built condition, whereas the aged alloy reveals additional peaks. The extra peaks are the superlattice reflection of the observed ordered Ni 3 (Ti, Al) L1 2 -structured phase (smaller particles) and L2 1 -structured phase (larger particles), as reported in earlier studies 12 , 25 , 26 . The estimated volume fractions of L1 2  and L2 1  phases are approximately 20% and 4%, respectively. The estimated lattice parameters of the fcc matrix phase, L1 2  precipitate, and L2 1  precipitate are 0.361, 0.369, and 0.585 nm, respectively. The average sizes of L1 2  and L2 1  phases estimated through the ImageJ software are 30 and 150 nm, respectively. The Modified Williamson–Hall plot (W–H plot) for both the alloys at the initial stage, considering pure-edge and pure-screw character dislocation contrast factor, is presented in Fig.  1d, e . The linear fitting on both alloys are fitted well, considering the pure-edge dislocation-contrast factor indicating dominant edge-dislocation character in both alloys 43 . The slope of linear fitting is higher for the aged alloy compared to the as-built alloy, indicating that the aged alloy has a higher dislocation density 43  due to the generation of GNDs to accommodate lattice-mismatch. The slight increment of dislocation even after ageing is due to the peak-ageing condition (i.e., no coarsening of precipitates) for the applied ageing time duration 44 , as reported peak hardness zone for the selected alloy 45 . The decreased  y -axis intercept of the aged alloy reflects a reduced coherently scattered crystallite size after precipitation ageing. Detailed calculation of parameters for the W–H plot is discussed in the Supplementary Note  N1 . Fig. 1 Initial microstructural-characterization of the Al 0.2 Co 1.5 CrFeNi 1.5 Ti 0.3  HEAs. SEM micrograph of the ( a ) as-built and  b  aged samples,  c  Rietveld-refined diffraction patterns of the as-built (blue) and aged (red) alloys before LCF loading,  d  Modified W–H plots at the initial stage by considering edge dislocations for the fcc slip system <110 > {111}.  e  Modified W–H plots at the initial stage by considering screw dislocation for the fcc slip system, <110 > {111}. (Numerical data for the plots are available in Supplementary Dataset  2 ).

sections.heading: Low-cycle fatigue stress profiles and fatigue life comparison
paragraphs: The maximum stress-evolution profile subjected to fully reversed strain-controlled, tension-compression cyclic loading at 0.30%, 0.50%, 0.75%, 1.00%, and 1.25% strain amplitudes for both as-built and aged alloys are presented in Fig.  2a . The obvious dependency of the increased cyclic-stress response (CSR) and decreased fatigue-life with increasing applied strain-amplitudes is evident in the stress-profile. The stress profiles of both alloys show almost constant or very mild softening at lower strain amplitudes, but show hardening-softening behavior with increasing strain amplitude. The observed hardening-softening in the as-built alloy above 0.50% strain amplitude is very similar, but hardening behavior is much more evident with increasing strain-amplitude in the aged alloy. The hardening and softening behaviors are usually related to dislocation multiplication and dislocation arrangement/annihilation, respectively. The observed increase in hardening with increasing strain amplitude of the aged alloy is consistent with the reported increasing density of slip-band formation with increasing strain amplitude 31 , 46 . The observed hardening-softening phenomenon has been described in the discussion section. The observed CSR of the aged alloy is substantially higher, as compared to the as-built alloy at all strain amplitudes, and the gap in the evolved stress profile is maintained throughout the loading till fracture. This trend is indicative of the strengthening effect of L1 2  and L2 1  precipitates during cyclic loading throughout the fatigue deformation. To highlight the status of the high loading capacity during the fatigue loading and the benefit of partial Al substitution by Ti, as mentioned for the Al–Ti fraction optimization 25  during the developmental stage of the selected alloy, the stress evolution profiles of recently published precipitation-strengthened Al 0.5 CoCrFeNi HEA 31  and Ni-based NIMONIC-90 superalloy 47  were also plotted in Fig.  2a . The comparison shows a promising and high fatigue-stress profile along with notable fatigue life for the selected HEA. The strain-amplitude vs fatigue-life comparison for different structural alloys subjected to completely reversed LCF at room temperature is shown in Fig.  2b  (data provided in Supplementary Dataset  1 ). It exhibits that the selected HEA alloys surpassed the fatigue life of many conventional alloys used in aerospace and power-plant industries at a strain amplitude lower than 0.50%. Overall, the studied alloy has notable fatigue life at lower strain amplitudes (below 0.50%) with a sufficiently high fatigue stress profile. These characteristics suggest the suitability of the selected material for lightweight applications and load spikes due to unwanted fluctuations with a sufficient safety margin. The comparative fatigue life trend between the as-built and aged alloys indicates an enhanced fatigue life of the aged alloy at lower strain amplitudes. Fig. 2 Low-cycle fatigue result of the Al 0.2 Co 1.5 CrFeNi 1.5 Ti 0.3  HEA. a  CSR curves of the Al 0.2 Co 1.5 CrFeNi 1.5 Ti 0.3  HEAs for the as-built (blue), aged (red), as well asAl 0.5 CoCrFeNi HEA (green) 31  and Nimonic 90 (purple) 47  at different strain amplitudes, (Adapted with permission from the work of Raman et al., International Journal of Fatigue, Volume 16, Issue 3, April 1994, Pages 209-215, Copyright 1994 Elsevier).  b  Comparison of strain-amplitude vs fatigue-life data for the present alloys with other conventional alloys and HEAs 31 , 33 , 37 , 76 , 81 ,  82 ,  83 ,  84 ,  85 ,  86 ,  87 ,  88 ,  89 ,  90 ,  91 ,  92 ,  93 ,  94 ,  95 ,  96 ,  97 – 98  subjected to completely-reversed LCF at room temperature (numerical data for the plots are available in Supplementary Datasets  1  and  2 ).

sections.heading: Models and analysis
Fatigue–fracture–surface investigation
paragraphs: Images in Fig.  4a, b  show the fractured surface of both as-built and aged alloys at a 0.50% strain amplitude. The fracture surface of the as-built alloy has three different regions: (i) crack-initiation, (ii) crack-propagation, and (iii) the final-rupture region. However, there is no such demarcation in the aged alloy. A closer look at different regions of the as-built fractured surface is presented in Fig.  4a  (1, 2, 3). Region 1 of the as-built alloy shows a crack initiated at the surface, attributed to the plastic-strain localization and some defects. Next to that, region 2 has striation marks, reflecting crack advancement with the fatigue cycle by closing and opening of a crack tip, and the dimples in region 3 indicate final ligament rupture as a ductile-fracture mode. The lateral surface near the fracture presented in Fig.  4c  shows conspicuous intrusion–extrusion patterns, which are commonly associated with cross-slip activity and have been reported to promote deformation irreversibility and surface strain localization 52 , 53 . This trend signifies wavy-slip behavior and the tendency toward surface damage. In the aged alloy, there are multiple crack-initiation signs at the surface, as well as at the interior, as presented in Fig.  4b . These observations are likely associated with strain-localization at L2 1  precipitates-matrix interfaces and intrinsic defects introduced during AM. Upon closer inspection, the entire region has tear ridges, and shear steps generally form due to interactions of various crack planes and micro-dimples throughout the surface. The observation indicates that the multiple initiated cracks join and fracture as a quasi-cleavage mode. The tearing ridges separating the facets resulted from the propagation of cracks on several planes. This undulating layered-cleavage evidencing crack hindering by blocky L2 1  precipitates 17 . The lateral-surface morphology of aged alloy presented in Fig.  4d, e  shows slip bands that suggest a more planar slip-dominated deformation mode. This observation indicates a decreased tendency for strain localization at the surface and surface damage. The comparative aspects of slip bands at different strain amplitudes of aged alloy (Fig.  4d, e ) show that the number of activated slip planes increases with increasing strain amplitude. This feature suggests that the increased initial hardening with strain amplitude may be related to a higher density of activated slip bands, consistent with forest-hardening mechanisms. A fractured-surface investigation of as-built alloy fractured at different strain amplitudes exhibits an increased width of striation with increasing the applied strain-amplitude (Supplementary Fig.  S3 a–c), which indicates a higher crack-growth rate. A magnified view near the surface in the aged alloy with increasing strain amplitude, presented in Supplementary Fig.  S3d–f  illustrate a transition in fracture mode from a transgranular fracture (characterized by tearing ridges through the grains) at low strain amplitudes to a mixed transgranular-intergranular pattern (featuring both cleavage within grains and cracking along grain boundaries) at higher strain amplitudes. This transition in fractured behavior may be associated with a shift from inhomogeneous to more homogeneous deformation with increasing strain amplitude. Fig. 4 Fractured and lateral surfaces of the fatigued Al 0.2 Co 1.5 CrFeNi 1.5 Ti 0.3  HEAs. SEM-fracture surfaces of different regions fatigued at a 0.50% strain amplitude in the ( a ) as-built and  b  aged samples, SEM images of a lateral surface in the ( c ) as-built, and  d ,  e  in the aged alloys.

sections.heading: Post-fatigue TEM investigation
paragraphs: Post-fatigue TEM observations revealing the microscopic-deformation mechanisms are presented in Fig.  5 . TEM images at various magnifications for the aged alloy subjected to strain amplitudes of 0.50%, 1.00%, and 1.25% are shown in Fig.  5a–c , respectively. At 0.50% strain amplitude, high-magnification imaging reveals the formation of dislocation walls. A closer inspection in Fig.  5 a2 highlights dislocation pile-ups at the interface between L2₁ and L1₂ precipitates. Further magnification in Fig.  5 a3 displays lattice fringes in the fcc matrix, indicative of dislocation structures formed through planar slip. In contrast, the samples fatigued at higher strain amplitudes of 1.00% and 1.25% exhibit twinning features, as shown in Fig.  5 b1, c1, and in the corresponding magnified views (b2), (c2). The detailed image in Fig.  5 b3 shows lattice fringes within the L1₂ precipitates and clear evidence of dislocation-induced shearing. Such precipitate shearing at elevated strain amplitudes is expected to facilitate dislocation glide 54 , 55 , and may contribute to the increased cyclic softening observed, as reflected in the CSR in Fig.  2a . At 1.25% strain amplitude, the magnified images in Fig.  5 c2, c3 reveal lattice fringes in multiple orientations, suggesting activation of planar slip across several slip systems. This multi-slip activity can lead to dislocation interactions such as Lomer–Cottrell locks, which are commonly associated with forest-hardening mechanisms during deformation. The transition from limited to multiple slip-system activation with increasing strain amplitudes may help explain the enhanced initial cyclic hardening observed at higher strain amplitudes as seen in Fig.  2a . Fig. 5 Post-fatigued TEM results of Al 0.2 Co 1.5 CrFeNi 1.5 Ti 0.3  -HEAs. TEM images of the aged alloy,  a  at a 0.50% strain amplitude;  b  at a 1.00% strain amplitude;  c  at a 1.25% strain amplitude; TEM images of the as-built alloy,  d  at a 1.00% strain amplitude.

Additionally, Fig.  5 d1 presents a TEM bright-field image of the as-built alloy fatigued at a 1.00% strain amplitude, showing dislocation accumulation at cell walls and dislocation traces within cells. The noticeable contrast between adjacent cells suggests lattice misorientation, indicating the formation of sub-grains. The dark-field image in Fig.  5 d2 highlights dislocation tangles within some cells and labyrinth-like structures in others, with an enlarged view of the tangles shown in Fig.  5 d3. The dislocation structures reflect retained cell walls in the as-built state, which act as partial barriers to dislocation motion, resulting in dislocation pile-up near boundaries. With continued cyclic deformation, dislocations within cells rearrange into low-energy configurations, contributing to cyclic softening. Moreover, features, such as dislocation tangles and labyrinth structures, are typically associated with cross-slip activity, suggesting a wavy-slip–dominated deformation mode in the as-built alloy 55 .

sections.heading: In situ neutron-diffraction investigation
paragraphs: The fatigue-deformation behavior and microstructural variation during cyclic deformation are quantitatively and qualitatively analyzed using line-profile-analysis (LPA) of in situ neutron-diffraction patterns conducted at 1.00% strain amplitude. The dislocation activity and the role of L1 2  precipitates under cyclic loading in the aged alloy are described through the in situ recorded diffraction-patterns. Figure  6a  shows the estimated phase fraction obtained through the Rietveld-refinement of diffraction patterns at the maximum tension and compression points specified in Fig.  10 . The phase fractions of all phases remain invariant throughout the fatigue loading. This trend indicates that the precipitates remained stable during cyclic-loading. The distribution of phases near fractured regions of post fatigue samples through SEM (Supplementary Fig.  S4a–c ) also demonstrates the phase stability during deformation. The consistent cyclic-strength gap between the corresponding aged and as-built alloys throughout the fatigue deformation can be attributed to the effective strengthening associated with the stable precipitates. Fig. 6 In situ neutron-diffraction results of the Al 0.2 Co 1.5 CrFeNi 1.5 Ti 0.3  HEAs. a  Phase fraction with the number of fatigue cycles,  b  hysteresis loops of different families of planes at the 1st cycle for the as-built alloy,  c  hysteresis loop of different families of planes at the 1st cycle for the aged alloy,  d  hysteresis loop of the FCC (111) and L1 2  (210) at 1st, 12th, and 250th cycles,  e  evolution of residual stress with progressing fatigue cycles in the fcc matrix and L1 2  precipitate after unloading from tension, and  f  stress evolution in the fcc matrix and L1 2  precipitate at tension and compression stages (numerical data for the plots are available in Supplementary Dataset  2 ).

The hysteresis-loop area and the strain levels of differently oriented families of grains, as presented in Fig.  6b, c , shows plastic-anisotropy among the grains. It indicates grain-to-grain yielding behavior with a higher load shared by (200) oriented grains. Figure  6d  shows the cyclic-hysteresis loop of the (210) plane of the L1 2  phase and (311) plane of the fcc matrix at the initial-stage, peak hardening-stage, and softening-stage. The comparative hysteresis-loop shows that the L1 2  phase is deformable and has a very close strain-compatibility with the fcc-matrix throughout the deformation. The observed deformable nature of the multi-component L1 2  precipitates suggests that they impede dislocation motion, which may enhance the damage tolerance and dislocation-storing capacity of the alloy, as reported under monotonic loading 18 . This behavior is expected to improve work hardenability and promote more uniform plastic deformation. The coherency and observed strain compatibility of the L1 2  precipitates with the matrix, which may reduce local stress/strain concentrations and thereby delay microcrack initiation during deformation 56 ,  57 ,  58 – 59 . Interactions at the microstructural level during deformation lead to the development of micro-stresses. Micro-stresses in multiphase materials are classified into intergranular stress, attributed to elastic and/or plastic anisotropy associated with preferred grain orientation, and phase stress, attributed to mismatches in phase properties 60 ,  61 – 62 . Inter-phase micro-stresses are induced to accommodate strain incompatibilities among the phases. These micromechanical interactions generate stress/strain heterogeneity during deformation at the micron level, leading to the propensity for micro-crack initiation 57 , 58 . The evolution of phases and grain-specific residual stresses, along with their stability during cyclic loading, plays an important role in load sharing and influences the tendency for fatigue-crack initiation. The residual-stress evolution with a progressing number of fatigue cycles in the fcc matrix and L1 2  precipitate are shown in Fig.  6e . The residual-stress profiles of matrix and L1 2  phase followed a very similar trend, which reflects aligned compatible deformation at the matrix-precipitate interface. During the initial cycles in the hardening zone, the residual stress is higher due to the early generation of dislocation pile-up (predicted through FWHM/d G  in Fig.  7b ). At the later stage, residual stress decreased and became constant with proceeding cycles. The decrease in residual stress may be associated with the rearrangement of dislocations into lower-energy configurations, as the trace of dislocation tangles observed through TEM 63 , 64 . Moreover, the reduction and saturation of the residual stress are also possibly due to micro-crack generation 63 . The compatible and simultaneous deformation of the matrix and L1 2  precipitate is also reflected in the stress-evolution profile during tension and compression, as presented in Fig.  6f . The required stress is estimated using Eq. ( 7 ) described in the materials and experimental procedure section. Fig. 7 Dislocation evolution, arrangement, and character during LCF in the matrix phase of the Al 0.2 Co 1.5 CrFeNi 1.5 Ti 0.3  HEAs. a  Evolution of FWHM G /d vs the number of cycles at a 1.00% strain amplitude for the as-built alloy,  b  evolution of FWHM G /d vs the number of cycles at a 1.00% strain amplitude for the aged alloy,  c  dislocation-arrangement parameter ( M ) variation with progressive deformation, and  d q  parameter showing the type of dislocation during deformation (numerical data for the plots are available in Supplementary Dataset  2 ).

The dislocation evolution and activity, which play a major role in the deformation and observed hardening-softening behavior, were estimated from diffraction-peak broadening. The Gaussian full-width at half-maximum (FWHM G ) component of the Pseudo–Voigt fitted peak has a proportional relation with the dislocation density 65  (described in Eqs. ( 8 ) and ( 9 ) in the experimental section). Figure  7a, b  show the FWHM G /d variation with fatigue cycles for the most representative (311) fcc peak 66  at the maximum tension and compression points subjected to a 1.00% strain-amplitude for the as-built and the aged alloys, respectively. The dislocation density profile of the aged alloy is comparatively higher than that of the as-built alloy throughout the deformation. This feature suggests an increased dislocation-storing capability, which may be associated with the presence of deformable multicomponent L1 2  precipitates, as mentioned by Yang et al. 18  under monotonic loading. FWHM G /d rapidly increases for the first few cycles in both aged and as-built samples during tension and compression stages. After a rapid increase, a little drop and saturation are observed for the later stage of cycles in the as-built alloy. The as-built alloy shows rapid dislocation multiplication during the initial cycles, resulting in material hardening. During the later cycles, the counterbalancing impact of dislocation-multiplication and dislocation rearrangement/annihilation leads to material softening. No rapid drop in the dislocation density until the late stage of cycles suggests the absence of significant damage accumulation at this stage, indicating a comparatively higher resistance to microcrack initiation.

The screening and arrangement of dislocation inside the materials can be described using the dislocation arrangement,  M -parameter ( M  =  R e* ρ 0.5 ), estimated through the CMWP procedure 65 . The variation of  M  with the progressing number of fatigue cycles is shown in Fig.  7c . The  M  value of the pre-deformed as-built sample is relatively high, indicating that the dislocations are randomly distributed inside the cell, in addition to the cell-wall region. The  M  value of the pre-deformed aged sample is relatively low, as compared to the as-built sample. This feature indicates that the dislocations are rearranged into a more dipolar configuration in addition to dislocation generation after precipitation ageing, which can be correlated with the decreased crystallite size observed in the W–H plot. During the initial cyclic deformation of the as-built alloy, the  M  value decreases, implying a shift of dislocations from a random distribution to a more organized configuration. Hence, the dislocation-evolution profile (FWHM G /d in Fig.  7a ) and  M  variation indicate that the hardening–softening transition during the initial cycles can be explained by a combined effect of dislocation multiplication and dislocation rearrangement. Variation of  M  in the aged alloy is not much during deformation, implying that dislocation multiplication plays a dominant role during initial hardening, and annihilation at later cycles leads to softening. Figure  7d  Dislocation character during deformation estimated through the CMWP ‘ q ’ parameter and presented in Fig.  7d . The  q  values for pure edge and pure screw characters were estimated from the theoretical calculation made by Ungar et al. 43  using Zener anisotropy ratio (2C 44 /C 11 –C 12 ) and C 12 /C 44  ratio for the selected material (The detailed calculation is presented in a Supplementary Note  N1  and Supplementary Fig.  S1 .). At the initial state, the  q  value is the same for both as-built and aged alloy, and approximately 80% edge and 20% screw characters. During deformation at the initial cycles, the fraction of screw dislocations increases in the as-built alloy, but the dislocation character of the aged alloy shifts to the pure edge dislocation. The dislocation distribution and arrangement during cyclic deformation are governed by dislocation glide patterns. Generally, cross-slip is mediated by screw dislocations while planar-slip is mediated by edge dislocations. The reduced SFE due to the elemental segregation as precipitates 67  and the increased anti-phase boundary (APB) energy of ordered-precipitate phases in the aged alloy hinder the merging of screw partial dislocations into perfect dislocations and increase the resistance to dislocation motion, respectively 55 . Hence, the shift of dislocation character toward a higher edge component in the aged alloy suggests a tendency toward planar-slip-dominated deformation, consistent with SEM and TEM observations. On the other hand, the dislocation character of the as-built alloy slightly shifted towards screw character, reflecting an increased contribution of cross-slip during deformation and suggesting a wavy-slip dominated deformation mode. The nearly constant M values in the aged alloy may be associated with a planar-slip–dominated deformation mode, while that in the as-built alloy is more, and several dislocation arrangements were observed on the TEM images shown in Fig.  5d .

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: The comparative observation of experimentally recorded fatigue-stress profile shows a significant strengthening contribution by the dual-precipitates while maintaining a remarkable fatigue life at lower strain-amplitudes compared to various structural alloys. The fatigue life of the as-built alloy is dominant above the 0.50% strain, while the fatigue life of the aged alloy dominates below 0.50%. The observed dominating fatigue property of aged alloy at lower strain amplitudes is associated with the planar-slip mode of deformation, as observed through SEM and TEM of the fatigued sample. Planar-slip is generally reported to be associated with a lower dislocation recovery rate and good deformation reversibility 54 , 55  and enhances fatigue strength and life. Although it has a planar-slip mode of deformation at higher strain amplitudes, several other factors, such as precipitate shearing, inherent AM defects, and microcracking at the L2 1  interface (Supplementary Fig.  S4 ) due to strain-localization, may shorten the fatigue life.

The stress-profile pattern of the as-built alloy does not have much variation with applied strain-amplitude and shows similar hardening-softening at all strain amplitudes except at a 0.30% strain amplitude. The initial hardening is due to the dislocation generation during initial cycles, and softening is due to the dislocation rearrangement and annihilation during later cycles, as reflected in the dislocation density profile and the dislocation arrangement  M  parameter estimated through an in situ neutron-diffraction experiment. The decreased fatigue-life and early hardening-softening transition with increasing strain-amplitude are related to the accelerated crack-propagation because of the higher applied strain-energy dissipation per cycle 68 . The increased striation spacing with increased strain-amplitude presented in Supplementary Fig.  S3  also reflects the higher crack-propagation rate. Quantitative estimation reveals that crack-initiation consumes a substantial amount of fatigue cycles. Hence, it can be inferred that the uniform-deformation process governs the substantial portion of fatigue-life while strain-localization and crack-initiation occur at a later stage of fatigue deformation. The lateral surface morphology indicates that plastic deformation is accommodated by wavy slip, resulting in the formation of persistent slip bands (PSBs) at the surface, which usually serve as sites for surface-crack initiation. Dislocation accumulation at the initial cell boundary observed through TEM shows that these initial dislocation cells act as soft barriers to dislocation motion, which does not fully stop the plastic-deformation governing dislocation partials but traps them temporarily 69 . Hence, it provides strengthening, as well as avoiding localized stress-concentration for crack-initiation. Dislocation motion can also be impeded by the coherent internal stress due to the lattice-misfit acquired by Al and Ti micro-segregation at the cell-boundary region (TEM-EDS presented in Supplementary Fig.  S5 ) 69 , 70 . The dislocation substructures inside the cell indicate that dislocation glides are mostly restricted within the cells and arranged into some low-energy configurations, as typically observed in wavy-slip materials 55 . The shifting towards a higher screw fraction through CMWP also reflects the dominating wavy slip.

In the aged alloy, hardening-softening behavior is dependent on strain-amplitude. There is almost no cyclic hardening during the initial cycles at lower strain-amplitudes while hardening is much more dominant with increasing strain amplitudes. The observed hardening behavior is consistent with the reported shifting of single to multiple slip activation and increased density of slip-band formation 31 , 46 , 71 . The combined effect of decreased SFE due to elemental segregation at precipitates and higher APB energy of ordered L1 2  precipitates is expected to favor planar-slip deformation 72 , 73 . As it has a planar-slip mode of deformation, the activation of a multiple-slip system provides forest hardening, as well as Lomer-Cottrell locks, as observed through TEM. Twinning at higher strain amplitudes also acts as barriers to dislocation movement and provides hardening. The increasing softening rate with the increasing strain-amplitude is also observed in the stress profile. Besides dislocation re-arrangement and annihilation, several other mechanisms are also proposed to describe the softening phenomena in precipitation-strengthened materials. These mechanisms involve inhomogeneous plastic-deformation caused by strain-localization, as well as precipitate-dissolution and precipitate-shearing 46 , 74 , 75 . At higher strain amplitudes, precipitation shearing was observed, which provides an easy glide path for dislocations, resulting in a comparatively higher softening rate. The dislocation rearrangement and dislocation annihilation at microcracks observed near L2 1  interfaces are the major reasons for softening 31 , 76 , 77 . The planar-slip mode of deformation is generally associated with enhanced deformation reversibility and strain uniformity. Hence, the value of damage-defusing capability (higher  β ) increased. However, due to twinning at higher strain amplitude, the strain-localization is higher and consequently, more susceptible to crack-initiation.

Overall, the plastic deformation in the as-built alloy appears to be dominated by wavy glides of dislocation. Due to slip irreversibility associated with wavy glide, conspicuous intrusion and extrusion were formed at the surface during deformation. Those intrusion-extrusions at the surface lead to crack-initiation with the subsequent cyclic deformation. The plastic deformation of the aged alloy appears to be dominated by planar glides of dislocation. At lower strain-amplitudes, dislocation activity is mostly restricted to the fcc matrix and piles up at the precipitate boundaries. With the increasing strain-amplitude, multiple-slip systems are activated and shear precipitates. At higher strain-amplitudes, twinning phenomena are also activated, which contribute to hardening, as well as act as strain-localized regions initiating microcracks. Strain-localization at the matrix-L2 1  interface also acts as a crack-initiation site, as several microcracks were observed at the interface, depicted in Supplementary Fig.  S4 . The dislocation- arrangement patterns during deformations and the impact of hysteresis-energy-model-based parameters are schematically described in Fig.  8 . Fig. 8 Summarized schematics of the cyclic-deformation behavior and parametric aspect of Al 0.2 Co 1.5 CrFeNi 1.5 Ti 0.3  HEAs.

In conclusion, leveraging emerging additive-manufacturing (AM) techniques in conjunction with precipitation-strengthening strategies offers a promising pathway for developing advanced fatigue-resistant HEAs. The additively manufactured HEAs with bimodal precipitate structures demonstrate strong potential for meeting fatigue resistance benchmarks, as the precipitates contribute to both mechanical strengthening and crack-growth resistance. The observed fatigue-life in the selected precipitation-strengthened AM-HEA crossed 10 4  and 10 5  cycles at 0.5% and 0.3% strain-amplitudes, respectively, while maintaining a reasonable stress-profile. Key findings from our study, such as the influence of AM-induced cellular structures and the deformable nature of multi-component L1₂ precipitates, provide valuable insights for tailoring and optimizing the fatigue performance of such materials. Future work incorporating detailed quantitative analyses of porosity, defect populations, and process-parameter optimization would further enable the decoupling of defect-controlled and microstructure-controlled fatigue mechanisms.

sections.heading: Sample fabrication
paragraphs: The specified composition of the Al 0.2 Co 1.5 CrFeNi 1.5 Ti 0.3  alloy has been printed layer by layer using a L-PBF technique employing a zig–zag scanning strategy with successive rotation of 67 °. The laser-process parameters included a laser power of 260 W, spot size of 58 μm, hatch spacing of 70 μm, and scanning speed of 1000 mm/s applied on a 50 μm powder layer in an argon atmosphere. The specified parameter is optimized to obtain the highest density, higher than 97%, as specified in the earlier published literature 26 . The specimens were built on a carbon steel plate preheated to 200 °C and removed using electrical discharge machining for subsequent investigations. The part of the L-PBF as-built sample was directly aged for 50 h at 750 °C to obtain the optimum precipitation, as specified by ref.  26 .

sections.heading: Mechanical testing and microstructural investigation
paragraphs: For LCF testing, specimens with specified dimensions as shown in Fig.  9 , were prepared from both the L-PBF as-built and aged blocks. Completely reversed tension-compression LCF tests were conducted at 0.30%, 0.50%, 0.75%, 1.00%, and 1.25% strain amplitudes with a triangular loading waveform under a continuous-loading condition. A materials test system (MTS) extensometer was used to measure all the strains. The pre-deformation and post-deformation microstructural features, distribution of precipitates, elemental-distribution mapping, and fatigued fracture surface were characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). For SEM, samples were ground, polished, and then electrochemically etched in 20 vol% phosphoric acid at 5 V for 15 s using a copper electrode. Microstructural features were quantitatively measured using the ImageJ software. Fig. 9 LCF sample dimension details.
